498.title: Can a mother forget? (Isaiah 49:15–16)
498.hook: even if she did, I will not forget you: engraved on my palms
498.howItsDone: Some churches read Isaiah 49:15–16 for comfort and on Mother's Day, and Christians point to it when describing God's love with a mother's tenderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shroud lifted at a feast for every nation, and death swallowed up. Your line: tears wiped away.

Three in the morning. A baby stirs in the next room, makes one small sound, and the mother is awake before she knows why. She can sleep through traffic, thunder, a neighbor's party. Not that sound. The body seems to keep listening even when the mind is off. It's about as close as everyday life gets to a love that can't forget. Now set beside it a whole people who feel completely forgotten: far from home, their city in ruins, their prayers going nowhere. And they say so, out loud, to God.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING, ONE SMALL SOUND.`

segments.voice: This part of Isaiah speaks to the people exiled in Babylon, and Jerusalem, called Zion, is pictured as a grieving woman. She says, in the King James Bible: "The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me." It's a raw line, and the Bible lets it stand. God answers with a question: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Not a king, not a judge: a nursing mother. Some readers point out that the Hebrew word for compassion is related to the word for womb, so the language itself carries a mother's body. Then the passage goes further. Even a mother's love can fail; the text admits it. God's memory is stronger than that. Then the second picture: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands." Graven means engraved, cut in, like letters in stone. Not a note on the back of a hand that washes off. A name carved into the palm, permanent, in the one place you see every time you reach for something. Jewish readers hear God's promise never to abandon Zion and its people. Christians read it that way too, and some also think of the wounds in Jesus's hands, palms that carry the mark of love. Either way, the answer to Zion's complaint isn't an argument. It's a hand, held up, with her name on it.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE GRAVEN THEE UPON THE PALMS OF MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Open your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at the lines, the creases, the marks of whatever work you've done. Picture there the name of someone you never want to forget, and then, if it fits, your own name carved in a palm you can't see, held by someone who remembers you. If you pray, rest in the promise, I will not forget thee; if not, notice what it feels like to be held in someone's memory.
Compassion. The Hebrew word that shares its root with womb, used for the care God says will not fail, even if a mother's might.
Your line: engraved on his hands. Not a note that washes off. See you tomorrow.

499.title: No balm in Gilead? (Jeremiah 8:18–22)
499.hook: the weeping prophet asks why his people aren't healed; later a spiritual answered, there is a balm
499.howItsDone: Christians sing the African American spiritual "There Is a Balm in Gilead," and some churches read Jeremiah 8 in services of lament and in prayers for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion: the care Isaiah says outlasts even a mother's, and a name carved on God's palms. Your line was engraved on his hands.

Some places are known for one thing. Champagne, Florida oranges, Swiss watches. In the Bible, it's balm from Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan River. It was a fragrant resin, prized as medicine for wounds. In Genesis, the caravan that buys young Joseph from his brothers is coming from Gilead, camels loaded with balm, bound for Egypt. In the Bible's world, Gilead meant medicine. So when the prophet Jeremiah wanted to say how bad things had become, he asked a question that would sound almost absurd.
screen: `SOME PLACES ARE KNOWN FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?" The medicine exists, the doctors exist, so why are my people still sick? Jeremiah has been nicknamed the weeping prophet, and this passage shows why. Just before it, he grieves: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." The season for rescue has come and gone. Just after, he wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, to weep day and night. Earlier in the chapter, he complains that other prophets were treating the people's wound lightly, saying "Peace, peace; when there is no peace." Jeremiah won't paper over the wound. He'd rather weep. And in these verses it's hard to tell who's speaking. Jeremiah, or God? The voices blur, as if God's grief and the prophet's are the same tears. Long after, an African American spiritual turned Jeremiah's question into an answer. The song begins: there is a balm in Gilead. Not is there. There is. In the song, the balm points to Jesus, the healer. People singing out of hard lives answered yes. The honest question and the answer belong together: tears that don't pretend, and hope that doesn't give up.
screen: then, large: `IS THERE NO BALM IN GILEAD?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is hurting, someone sick or grieving, someone whose wound others treat lightly, and don't rush to fix it in your head; let Jeremiah's question stand for a moment. Then picture a balm laid gently on that wound: rest, care, a doctor's skill, a friend's presence. If you pray, pray for their healing in your own words; if not, hold them in your attention with care, and think of one way to bring a little balm.
Weeping prophet. Jeremiah's nickname, earned by grief like this: asking why his people stay wounded when the medicine already exists.
Your line: there is a balm. Not a fix, but something soothing laid on a wound. Go gently.

500.title: Reading the prophets as Christians
500.hook: the church reads the prophets two ways at once: justice now and hope in Christ
500.howItsDone: In many churches, readings from the prophets are paired with Gospel readings in the lectionary, so Christians hear the prophets both as promises fulfilled in Christ and as a call to justice; many denominations ground their social ministries in passages like Isaiah 61 and Luke 4.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the weeping prophet, and a spiritual's answer to his question. Your line was there is a balm.

Day five hundred. For five weeks this path has been in the prophets: a burning coal on Isaiah's lips, a potter's wheel, dry bones, a man in a fish, a king on a donkey. When Christians read these books, are they reading about ancient Israel, or about Jesus? Is Amos about corrupt judges eight centuries before Christ, or about today? The answer the church has usually given: yes. All of it, at once. And the clearest place to watch it happen is a small synagogue in Nazareth, on an ordinary Sabbath.

Luke chapter four. Jesus comes home to Nazareth and goes to the synagogue on the Sabbath, as he usually did. Someone hands him the scroll of Isaiah. He unrolls it and finds the place: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Good news for the poor, sight for the blind, freedom for captives and the bruised. Then, in the King James Bible: "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." You can feel the silence. Then: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." That's the first way Christians read the prophets: looking for Christ. The suffering servant, the child born, the king on a donkey: Christians see these promises coming true in Jesus. But look at what Isaiah actually promises. Food for the poor. Freedom. Healing. Not only spiritual ideas. So the second way: as a call to justice, right now. Amos's river, Micah's three things, Jeremiah's tears. Churches that run soup kitchens and churches that write commentaries on fulfillment are often reading the same pages. Different churches lean on one way more, and many hold both. And plainly: these books were Israel's first. Jews have read the prophets for millennia, in their own way, and still do. Christians read them as Jesus did, as a Jew in a synagogue, with a scroll in his hands.
screen: `HE SAT DOWN, AND EVERY EYE WAITED.`
then, large: `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read Luke 4:16 to 21 slowly; if not, let the words come back: good news to the poor, healing for the brokenhearted, freedom for captives, sight for the blind. Then hold two questions: where in my town are the poor, the captives, the bruised, and where in my own life do I need good news? If you pray, read the verses as a prayer; if not, simply let the words sit.
Semeron, Greek for today, the first word of Jesus' answer in the Nazareth synagogue.
Your line: today it is fulfilled. Two ways of reading, one scroll. Five hundred days, and still walking.

501.title: Block close: the voices
501.hook: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a donkey king
501.howItsDone: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many people keep a single line from them, on a card, a wall or in memory, as a word to live by.

segments.voice: Yesterday, semeron, today, and the two ways Christians read the prophets. Your line was today it is fulfilled.

Isaiah's lips are still stinging from a burning coal. Jeremiah, who said he was too young, has clay from the potter's house on his sleeves. Ezekiel has heard dry bones rattle together in a valley. Daniel is fresh from the lions. Amos is still in his herdsman's clothes. Jonah is in a corner, sulking. Hosea is talking about his children. Zechariah is describing a king on a donkey. Habakkuk argued with God and came down singing. All in one room: loud, strange, brave, often unwelcome. Today, before the page turns, hear them all together.

The Hebrew word for prophet is navi, and the Bible shows the job. When Moses protests he can't speak well, God makes his brother Aaron his prophet, to say what Moses gives him. Not a fortune teller. A spokesperson. What did they say? To kings: you're not above the law. To festival crowds: your songs are noise while the poor are sold for a pair of shoes. To exiles in Babylon: comfort, you are mine, I have carved your name on my palms. To a people in rubble: a bag with holes, and build. To the hopeless: these bones can live; your old men shall dream dreams. Two notes, over and over: warning and comfort, justice and hope. Several pushed back on the job, like Moses. Jeremiah said he was only a child. Jonah paid his fare on a ship going the other way. Amos told a priest he was no prophet, just a herdsman taken from following the flock. Isaiah says here am I, send me, but only after a coal has touched his lips. They spoke anyway. Jeremiah said that when he tried to keep quiet, the word was like a fire shut up in his bones. Christians hear the prophets pointing forward to Jesus, who read their scroll in Nazareth and said today. Some also hear them pointing outward, to every place where a hard truth still needs saying. Tomorrow Luke's Gospel begins, with voices that sound like the prophets.
screen: `A FIRE SHUT UP IN THE BONES.`

Keep the one that lingers, and say it slowly until you know it by heart. If you pray, offer it back to God; if not, simply keep it.
Navi, Hebrew for prophet, a spokesperson for God: often reluctant messengers with two notes, warning and comfort, justice and hope.
Your line: someone has to say it. A true thing, said gently and clearly. That's the prophets, done.

502.title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
502.hook: Luke, a careful researcher, writes to Theophilus, friend of God
502.howItsDone: Some Christians read a Gospel straight through, a chapter a day, and churches following the common lectionary read mainly from Luke in one year of their three-year cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, navi: the prophets as spokespeople, with warning and comfort. Your line was someone has to say it. Today a new block begins.

For the next ninety days, this path does something simple and rare: it reads one Gospel, Luke, from beginning to end, in order. Not just the famous bits. The whole thing. And Luke starts like no other Gospel. Mark begins with a shout in the wilderness. John begins in eternity: in the beginning was the Word. Matthew begins with a family tree. Luke begins like a careful researcher writing a cover letter: how he worked, where his material came from, and why he's writing. Four verses, and you can almost hear him tapping his notes into a neat pile.

Here's how it opens, in the King James Bible: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us." Luke admits others have written about Jesus already. Then his sources: those "which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word." Then his method: he writes as one "having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first," setting it down in order. And his purpose: "That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed." Notice who he's writing to: most excellent Theophilus. Nobody knows for sure who he was. Most excellent is the title the book of Acts gives a Roman governor, Felix, so Theophilus may have been a person of rank. But his name means friend of God, or loved by God, and some readers wonder whether Luke means every reader who loves God. Either way, Luke wrote him a second volume: Acts opens with his name again. And who was Luke? The Gospel never names its author. Early Christian tradition says it was Luke, a physician and traveling companion of Paul, and the letter to the Colossians, under Paul's name, mentions Luke, the beloved physician. Some hold that tradition firmly; others weigh it differently. What the text itself shows is the method. Luke wants Theophilus to know this isn't rumor: he followed it all from the start.
screen: then, large: `THAT THOU MIGHTEST KNOW THE CERTAINTY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that happened to you that you don't want to lose: a conversation, a kindness, a turning point, something a grandparent told you. Walk through it from the beginning, in order, the way Luke gathered what the eyewitnesses said: who was there, what was said, what it changed. If you pray, give thanks for that moment; if not, simply hold it with care.
Theophilus, meaning friend of God: the man Luke writes to, with a careful, researched telling of Jesus, set down in order from the eyewitnesses.
Your line: so you may know. A careful telling, so a friend of God could be sure. Day five hundred two.

503.title: Zechariah in the temple (Luke 1:5–17)
503.hook: an old priest's prayer is answered at last in the holy place
503.howItsDone: Some churches read the story of Zechariah in the weeks before Christmas, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor Zechariah and Elizabeth as saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theophilus, friend of God, and Luke's careful, orderly account. Your line was so you may know.

Luke's story doesn't open in a palace, or even in Nazareth. It opens with an elderly couple who have done everything right. In the King James Bible: "There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias." That's the Greek form of Zechariah. His wife Elisabeth is from a priestly family too. Both righteous, Luke says, walking in all the commandments blameless. Then the line that hurts: "they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years." Good people. Faithful people. And the one thing they prayed for never came.

Zechariah's priestly division is on duty in Jerusalem, and by lot, the custom of the priest's office, he is chosen to go into the temple of the Lord and burn incense. Jewish tradition later recorded that a priest might get that honor only once in his life. So an old man stands alone at the altar of incense, smoke rising, while outside the whole crowd prays. Suddenly an angel is standing at the right side of the altar. Zechariah is terrified. The angel's first words: "Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Which prayer? Probably the one for a child, prayed for decades, maybe given up on years ago. Some readers also hear the prayer for Israel's rescue he was offering that very hour. Some hear the names too: Zechariah is usually taken to mean the LORD has remembered, and John, God is gracious. Then the child's job: to go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children." That echoes the closing lines of Malachi, heard seven days ago, the last book of the prophets in Christian Bibles. In Luke's telling, that waiting is over. Christians hear the whole Gospel starting here: not with fanfare, but with a faithful old man whose prayer was heard.
screen: `THE LOT FALLS: INCENSE IN THE HOLY PLACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you hoped or prayed for long ago and quietly stopped asking about: a healing, a reconciliation, a child, a door that never opened. Take it out and look at it again, the way Zechariah might have with the incense rising, and notice whether there's hope in you, or tiredness, or both. If you pray, offer that old prayer to God again, as honestly as you can; if not, hold the hope gently for these minutes.
Zechariah, usually taken to mean the LORD has remembered: the old priest told, fear not, thy prayer is heard.
Your line: your prayer is heard. An old man, an old prayer, and the Gospel begins. See you tomorrow.

504.title: Struck silent (Luke 1:18–25)
504.hook: he doubts and can't speak for nine months; Elizabeth hides and rejoices
504.howItsDone: Some Christians keep times of silence as a way of waiting, especially in Advent, and some monastic rules, like Saint Benedict's, make silence part of daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah, an old priest told, fear not. Your line was your prayer is heard.

An angel has just promised Zechariah the son he and Elisabeth prayed for. And what does he say? Not thank you. Not finally. In the King James Bible: "Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years." How can I be sure? It's such a human reply. After that long, hope can feel dangerous. Good news arrives, and the first move is to look for the catch. But this messenger is not amused. He tells Zechariah exactly who he is.

"I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings." Then the sign Zechariah asked for, though not the one he wanted: "thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed." Dumb, in older English, means unable to speak. Outside, the crowd wonders why he's taking so long. When he comes out, he can't say a word, only make signs with his hands. Near the end of Luke's Gospel, Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his friends. Some readers see the Gospel opening with a blessing that couldn't be spoken, and closing with one that is. Zechariah goes home in silence, and Elisabeth conceives. She hides herself five months, and says: "Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men." Reproach is her own word for the way people had looked at her. Now the Lord has looked on her. She keeps it close. So the house is quiet: a man who can't speak, a woman who won't, and a child growing in the silence. Christians read Zechariah's silence more than one way: as a consequence of doubt, and as a gift, months to listen instead of talk. This week has come a long way: a mother who can't forget, a balm, a scroll in Nazareth, the prophets' voices, Luke's careful letter, an old priest's prayer, and a quiet house where something is growing.
screen: then, large: `THOU SHALT BE DUMB, AND NOT ABLE TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Let the silence be as complete as you can; when words start up in your head, notice them and let them pass, like Zechariah's crowd outside the door. Then think of one place you usually fill with words, a meeting, an explanation, advice nobody asked for, and picture leaving a little more quiet there. If you pray, offer your silence to God as a kind of listening; if not, simply rest in the quiet.
Struck silent. Zechariah asks for proof and loses his voice until the promise comes true, while Elisabeth quietly carries the child.
Your line: silence can grow things. Quiet months, and a promise growing. Another week on the path.
